**A displacement is unusual relative to the data's usual scale and direction.** A change of ten units in a feature whose standard deviation is 100 is small; the same change in a feature whose standard deviation is one is large. Euclidean distance ignores that unless features are transformed. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

Mahalanobis distance accounts for the covariance matrix. With diagonal covariance, it divides squared coordinate differences by their variances. With correlated features, it also recognizes that movement along a common trend is less surprising than movement across a tight relationship.

Imagine height and weight are strongly correlated. A point moving along the tall-and-heavy direction can be ordinary even with a large raw distance from the mean. A mismatched height-weight combination can be unusual despite a smaller raw distance.

**The covariance estimate is part of the model.** Few samples, high dimension, or outliers can make its inverse unstable or misleading. Use shrinkage or a justified lower-dimensional representation and stable factorization-based solves. One ellipsoid also cannot describe every multimodal distribution. Mahalanobis distance improves the metric when its covariance assumptions match the data, not by universally replacing Euclidean distance.

**Technical details and references.**

Mahalanobis distance measures displacement after accounting for covariance, equivalent to Euclidean distance in whitened coordinates when covariance is positive definite. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

$$d_M(x,\mu)=\sqrt{(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}.$$

A displacement along a high-variance correlated direction is less surprising than the same raw displacement across a tight direction. Estimating covariance can be unstable when dimension is large relative to samples; use shrinkage or a justified low-rank model. Outliers can distort ordinary covariance, and a single Gaussian ellipsoid may not represent multimodal data. Solve using a factorization rather than explicitly inverting the matrix.
